title: Measurement Types
text:
Gain (similar to voltage on certain cytometers) is an unit which detected signal is amplified by for each detector. An instrument applies different gains to each detector, allowing for use of dim and bright fluorophores. During the Daily QC, these gains normally get minor adjustments to keep the QC beads’ signal constant, allowing for comparison of .fcs files acquired on different days. As the individual lasers in the cytometer are used, they slowly wear down and more gain is applied to remain at that setpoint. This contributes to the slowly increasing view typical of the gain plots:





Generally, when a laser is begining to rapidly wear out, we see steeper increases in the Gain plots. When the field service engineer replaces the laser, the gain values are reset according to the new laser. In this example, you can see that pattern for the violet laser of the instrument was replaced twice (red lines indicating field service engineer visit):





For the Cytek instruments, a Daily QC fail is triggered when the Gain is >100% of the original baseline Gain value. When this happens, a red flag is added to that timepoint. We have observed that .fcs files acquired on gain spike days (as seen below) may still have altered unmixing even if they have not exceeded the >100% threshold, so it’s worth keeping an eye on.








The robust coefficient of variation (rCV) is a measure of the resolution between the positive and negative population for each detector. When the value is high, dim staining populations may be harder to distinguish from the negative population. For spectral instruments where entire spectrum is used to identify a fluorophore, increased rCV on the detector where a fluorophore has its main peak has impacted unmixing for users with larger panels (>20 fluorophores). The RCV plots will typically resemble the following:





For Cytek instruments, a Daily QC fail is only triggered when %rCV exceeds either 8% for SSC, or 6% for FSC and the following detectors: UV3, V3, B3, YG3, R3. When this happens, the instrument will appear as failed on the home page:





When we navigate to the History tab and find that date, we can see that the rCV for UV3 failed, which was what triggered the QC fail:





But what happens if the RCV fails on any of the other detectors (UV1-> UV2, UV4 -> UV16,etc.)? Since they are not the indicator detectors, they won’t trigger a Cytek QC fail. However, since we have observed unmixing issues when the RCVs of these other detectors are exceeded, we don’t want to ignore them. Consequently, when a non-indicator RCV fails, we show it as failed under the Daily View:





And label the instrument as caution for that given day:





How to interpret these Caution notices depends on what we see in the Levey-Jennings plots. For a few detectors (especially UV1/UV2), they exceed the 6% cutoff but are stable over time. Consequently, the impact of the increased RCV is relatively minimal.





By contrast, is the RCV went from consistently stable, to spiking, the impact on your unmixing is likely to be significantly greater.

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text: Secondary QC for the Cytek Aurora EVO from SPHERO URCP-38-2K Ultra Rainbow beads. The set resolves into 6 populations — blank particles (peak 1) plus 5 fluorescent rainbow levels (peaks 2–6). Note on the Aurora: daily QC adjusts each APD’s gain to pin bead MFI to a target, so raw MFI is held ~constant by design — the informative signals are the ones gain can’t compensate: sensitivity (Q & B), resolution, %CV, linearity, and spectral-signature stability. Heavy FCS processing is done once by scripts/Process6PeakUltra.R; this page reads the peak_metrics.csv archive (+ the daily-QC gain) so it stays light.

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text:
Peak clustering
The 6 URCP-38-2K populations are assigned once per run by model-based clustering (flowClust, K = 6) on the asinh-transformed anchor detectors, then read out in every detector. This is far more robust than per-detector peak finding: weak channels can’t resolve dim peaks alone, but the strong anchor detectors can, and a bead’s population label is fixed across all detectors. Labels are ordered 1–6 by ascending brightness: peak 1 = blank particles, peaks 2–6 = fluorescent rainbow levels. Clustering runs in Process6PeakUltra.R; this page reads the persisted result.

2D cluster assignment (V8-A × B9-A)
The per-run diagnostic: each run’s gated beads shown on two detectors that both resolve all 6 peaks. A clean assignment shows 6 tight, ordered, single-coloured blobs along the diagonal — blank (peak 1) at the dim end, brightest (peak 6) at the top — with no interleaving.

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text:
Tracking over time
Each peak’s median intensity and %CV against acquisition timestamp — the QC payoff. Stable lines mean stable performance; a step or drift flags a detector/laser problem. Resolved, in-range peaks only. These fill in as runs accumulate (sparse, mostly points, with few timestamps so far).

Per-laser overview
Two 5-laser × run heatmaps of peak-6 deviation from each detector’s baseline (first run), averaged across the laser. Top: median intensity shift (blue = dimmer, red = brighter). Bottom: %rCV shift (blue = tighter, red = broader). A whole-row shift points to a laser-level issue; an isolated tile flags a single detector.


Code
p6_base <- pm |> filter(peak == n_peaks, in_range) |> group_by(detector) |>
  slice_min(run_label, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  transmute(detector, base_median = median) |> ungroup()
laser_delta <- pm |> filter(peak == n_peaks, in_range) |>
  left_join(p6_base, by = "detector") |>
  mutate(delta_pct = (median - base_median) / base_median * 100,
         laser = factor(laser_of(detector), levels = laser_levels)) |>
  group_by(laser, run_label) |> summarise(delta_pct = mean(delta_pct, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
lim <- max(abs(laser_delta$delta_pct), na.rm = TRUE); if (!is.finite(lim) || lim == 0) lim <- 1
gp(ggplot(laser_delta, aes(run_label, laser, fill = delta_pct,
        text = sprintf("%s laser | %s<br>%+.1f%% vs baseline", laser, run_label, delta_pct))) +
     geom_tile(colour = "white") +
     scale_y_discrete(limits = rev(laser_levels)) +
     scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0,
                          limits = c(-lim, lim), name = "Peak 6\nΔ median\nvs t0") +
     labs(title = "Per-laser peak-6 median deviation from baseline", x = NULL, y = "Laser") +
     theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
     theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 10)), 420)

title: 6 Peak Ultra Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text:
Staining index
Sensitivity over time: how far the first resolved peak above the blank sits above peak 1 (blank particles), relative to the blank’s spread — the classical detector-sensitivity benchmark, \(\mathrm{SI} = (\widetilde{m}_{\text{pos}} - \widetilde{m}_1)/(2\,\widetilde{\sigma}_1)\). Point colour marks which peak was used as the positive (it falls back from peak 2 toward peak 6 in weak detectors); a change in that reference for a detector is worth a look. A trend that drops = rising background or falling gain. The cross-detector snapshot is the SI heatmap under Resolution & SI.

text:
Sensitivity (Q & B) · in development






Warning



In development. The Q/B sensitivity model, MEF calibration, linearity, and gain context below are still being validated against the URCP-38-2K bead lot — treat as preliminary, not yet for routine QC decisions.


Q = detection efficiency (photoelectrons per unit signal, gain-normalised) — a drop means the detector collects less light per event. B = background/noise term; intrinsic CV = the high-signal noise floor (bead + optics), measured as the brightest resolved peak’s CV. Q and B are estimated per detector from the intrinsic-corrected CV² vs 1/MFI across the resolved peaks. Because Q = 1/slope blows up when the slope nears zero, fits that are ill-conditioned — near-flat slope, R² < 0.8, a non-monotonic CV profile, or a brightest-peak CV > 15% — are suppressed (left blank) rather than reported as a phantom Q spike; the underlying cause then shows in the %CV panel. Separately, runs whose beads fail the photon-domination check (dim-peak CV < 2× the bright peak, or dim-peak SD < 3× the blank; Chase 1998) are kept but flagged advisory — on spectral rainbow beads many runs fall short of that ideal, so those Q/B are lower-confidence rather than wrong.






NoteMethod & provenance — read me





This is the Q–B detector-sensitivity model of Hoffman & Wood (Wood JC, Cytometry 1998;33:260–266; Wood & Hoffman, Cytometry 1998;33:256–259; Chase & Hoffman, Cytometry 1998;33:267–279; Hoffman & Wood, Current Protocols in Cytometry Unit 1.20, 2007), the same model behind Spherotech’s STN-17 and BD’s CS&T Qr/Br. Total spread decomposes as CV² = CV_intr² + (1/Q)(1/S) + (B/Q)(1/S²). Following Hoffman & Wood, the intrinsic CV is taken directly from the brightest resolved peak and subtracted; the intrinsic-corrected CV² is then fit vs 1/S through the origin, giving 1/Q (linear term) and B/Q (curvature).
The panel-wide values use gain-normalised MFI (S = MFI/gain), not MEF, so Q and B are a relative, non-normalised index — valid for single-detector trend monitoring (Levey-Jennings), not cross-detector comparison, and expect small steps when a bead lot changes. Absolute, gain-independent sensitivity lives in the MEF-unit Q/B and detection-limit (MEF) panels below, on the anchor detectors.
Two method caveats (Hoffman & Wood 2007). (1) Linear scale. The Q/B model assumes photoelectron (Poisson) statistics on a linearly-amplified signal; Aurora MFI and robust CV are taken on the linear scale, which satisfies this — log-amp data would make B in particular unreliable. (2) Red / far-red detectors. Hoffman notes dim Rainbow beads can carry too high an intrinsic CV to give valid Q/B on red-laser channels; URCP-38-2K spans a wider range, but the same spectral-mismatch caution applies, so read red / far-red Q/B with extra care.

The regression above uses the resolved fluorescent peaks (the blank is used only as the blank). As an independent check, the literal STN-17 closed form uses just three populations — the blank (Dim Bead 1 = peak 1), one dim bead, and the brightest. text: Secondary QC for the Cytek Aurora EVO from RCP-30-5A 8-peak beads. Note on the Aurora: daily QC adjusts each APD’s gain to pin bead MFI to a target, so raw MFI is held ~constant by design — the informative signals are the ones gain can’t compensate: sensitivity (Q & B), resolution, %CV, linearity, and spectral-signature stability. Heavy FCS processing is done once by scripts/Process8Peak.R; this page reads the peak_metrics.csv archive (+ the daily-QC gain) so it stays light.

title: 8 Peak Bead Tracking — Aurora EVO (5L)
text:
Peak clustering
The 8 RCP-30-5A populations are assigned once per run by model-based clustering (flowClust, K = 8) on the asinh-transformed anchor detectors, then read out in every detector. This is far more robust than per-detector peak finding: weak channels can’t resolve the dim peaks alone, but the strong anchor detectors can, and a bead’s population is fixed across all detectors. Labels are ordered 1–8 by ascending brightness. Clustering runs in Process8Peak.R; this page reads the persisted result.

2D cluster assignment (V1-A × YG1-A)
The per-run diagnostic: each run’s gated beads shown on two detectors that both resolve all 8 peaks. A clean assignment shows 8 tight, ordered, single-coloured blobs along the diagonal, with no interleaving.

Tracking over time
Each peak’s median intensity and %CV against acquisition date — the QC payoff. Stable lines mean stable performance; a step or drift flags a detector/laser problem. Resolved, in-range peaks only. These fill in as runs accumulate (sparse, mostly points, with few dates so far).

Per-laser overview
Two 5-laser × date heatmaps of peak-8 deviation from each detector’s baseline (first run), averaged across the laser. Top: median intensity shift (blue = dimmer, red = brighter). Bottom: %rCV shift (blue = tighter, red = broader). A whole-row shift points to a laser-level issue; an isolated tile flags a single detector.

  left_join(p8_base, by = "detector") |>

  group_by(laser, date) |> summarise(delta_pct = mean(delta_pct, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

Staining index
Sensitivity over time: how far the first resolved peak above the blank sits above peak 1, relative to peak 1’s spread — the classical detector-sensitivity benchmark, \(\mathrm{SI} = (\widetilde{m}_{\text{pos}} - \widetilde{m}_1)/(2\,\widetilde{\sigma}_1)\). Point colour marks which peak was used as the positive (it falls back from peak 2 to 3, 4 … in weak detectors); a change in that reference for a detector is worth a look. A trend that drops = rising background or falling gain. The cross-detector snapshot is the SI heatmap under Resolution & SI.

text:
Sensitivity (Q & B) · in development






Warning



In development. The Q/B sensitivity model, MEF calibration, linearity, and gain context below are still being validated — treat as preliminary, not yet for routine QC decisions.


Q = detection efficiency (photoelectrons per unit signal, gain-normalised) — a drop means the detector collects less light per event. B = background/noise term; intrinsic CV = the high-signal noise floor (bead + optics), measured as the brightest resolved peak’s CV. Q and B are estimated per detector from the intrinsic-corrected CV² vs 1/MFI across the resolved peaks. Because Q = 1/slope blows up when the slope nears zero, fits that are ill-conditioned — near-flat slope, R² < 0.8, a non-monotonic CV profile, or a brightest-peak CV > 15% (e.g. a laser-instability run) — are suppressed (left blank) rather than reported as a phantom Q spike; the underlying cause then shows in the %CV panel. Separately, runs whose beads fail the photon-domination check (dim-peak CV < 2× the bright peak, or dim-peak SD < 3× the blank; Chase 1998) are kept but flagged advisory — on spectral rainbow beads many runs fall short of that ideal, so those Q/B are lower-confidence rather than wrong.






NoteMethod & provenance — read me





This is the Q–B detector-sensitivity model of Hoffman & Wood (Wood JC, Cytometry 1998;33:260–266; Wood & Hoffman, Cytometry 1998;33:256–259; Chase & Hoffman, Cytometry 1998;33:267–279; Hoffman & Wood, Current Protocols in Cytometry Unit 1.20, 2007), the same model behind Spherotech’s STN-17 and BD’s CS&T Qr/Br (BD app note “Qr and Br in BD FACSDiva Software”, 2012). Total spread decomposes as CV² = CV_intr² + (1/Q)(1/S) + (B/Q)(1/S²). Following Hoffman & Wood, the intrinsic CV is taken directly from the brightest resolved peak (its high-signal floor) and subtracted; the intrinsic-corrected CV² is then fit vs 1/S through the origin, giving 1/Q (linear term) and B/Q (curvature) — algebraically identical to BD’s SD² = (1/Q)·S + B/Q fit with Q = 1/slope, and to STN-17’s closed form (which subtracts the same bright-bead CV).
These panel-wide values use gain-normalised MFI (S = MFI/gain), not MESF, so Q and B are a relative, non-normalised index — not absolute MESF units. This is deliberate and is the intended use: BD reports its own Qr/Br in relative ABD units, and explicitly states that non-normalised Qr “values are still valid and serve as a powerful metric for tracking changes in detector performance over time” — a 50% change in a non-normalised Qr equals a 50% change in a normalised one. So treat these for single-detector trend monitoring (Levey-Jennings), not for cross-detector or cross-instrument comparison, and expect small steps when a bead lot changes. Absolute, gain-independent sensitivity lives in the MEF-unit Q/B and detection-limit (MEF) panels below, on the anchor detectors.
Two method caveats (Hoffman & Wood 2007). (1) Linear scale. The Q/B model assumes photoelectron (Poisson) statistics on a linearly-amplified signal; Aurora MFI and robust CV are taken on the linear scale, which satisfies this — log-amp data would make B in particular unreliable. (2) Red detectors. Hoffman notes the dim Rainbow (RCP-30-5A) beads carry too high an intrinsic CV to give valid Q/B on red-laser detectors, so red-channel Q/B — including the APC (R1-A) and APC-Cy7 (R7-A) MEF anchors — should be read with extra caution.



Fold-change maps: beside each absolute map, a companion normalises every detector to its own reference, stripping out absolute magnitude so dim and bright detectors are directly comparable and the colour isn’t dominated by the few brightest. The reference has two modes (set by fc_ref_window in the load chunk):

Dynamic / preliminary (current): reference = each detector’s best run so far. Good while characterising, but it shifts retroactively as runs accumulate, so it can’t anchor a stable trend.
Locked: once ~8–10 qualified runs exist, set fc_ref_window to a date range of known-good runs. The per-detector robust centre (median) ± SD over that window is frozen to data/reference/EVO_8peak_reference.csv, and the maps switch to a two-sided deviation-from-qualified-normal view (red = worse, in log₂ and SD units) where real drift and control-limit breaches emerge against a fixed anchor.
